power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

text.text: Within two years, an infant who can barely lift her head learns to sit, reach, and walk.

Developmental science found that this growth is both continuous and phased: skills improve smoothly, yet the pace of improvement changes at identifiable ages, and the field built statistical tools to locate those changes.
Language models also transform across training, and whether their capabilities grow smoothly or in jumps is actively debated.
The present study argues that the developmental answer applies to artificial learners as well, and that the developmental tools can show it.
We apply an analysis pipeline built for infant motor development to the training trajectories of 16 open-source language models, each tested at 27 points during training on five benchmarks.
The results mirror the infant findings.
Growth is continuous but organized into phases, and transitions cluster at a small set of shared points that are deployed differently across domains.
Growth proceeds slowly, then rapidly, then slowly, and models differ reliably in developmental rate.
Unlike infants, those rate differences are almost entirely explained by model size.
The transitions also survive changes of measurement scale, and on a continuous measure they appear earlier and more sharply than on accuracy.

The paper contributes a formal test for phase structure in capability growth, a construct mapping between infant development and language model development, and evidence that phase structure may be a shared property of learning systems.
Can LLMs Grow Like Children?
text.formatted: <head>Can LLMs Grow Like Children?

text.text: A Developmental Analysis of Capability
text.formatted: A Developmental Analysis of Capability</head>

text.text: At some point between the first and the last of 143,000 training steps, a large language model (LLM) that cannot complete a sentence becomes one that answers science questions and follows a story to its final word.
That path is observable.
Language models are trained by practicing next-word prediction on enormous amounts of text, and copies of the model, called checkpoints, can be saved along the way.
Each checkpoint can be tested on standardized benchmarks, fixed sets of questions administered identically every time, so a capability can be traced as a curve across training.
The shape of that curve is now the subject of an active debate.
One side describes the curve as smooth.
Scaling laws show that performance improves as a predictable function of a model's size, its training data, and the computation spent on training (Kaplan et al., 2020).
text.formatted: Scaling laws show that performance improves as a predictable function of a model's size, its training data, and the computation spent on training <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">(Kaplan et al., 2020)</ref>.

text.text: A single equation summarizes an enormous range of training runs, but it cannot represent periods of faster and slower change, and later work found that scaling curves often contain breaks (Caballero et al., 2023).
text.formatted: A single equation summarizes an enormous range of training runs, but it cannot represent periods of faster and slower change, and later work found that scaling curves often contain breaks <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">(Caballero et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: The other side describes the curve as discontinuous.

Studies of emergent abilities catalogue capabilities that appear absent in smaller or less-trained models and then present, sharply, in larger or further-trained ones (Srivastava et al., 2022; Wei et al., 2022).
text.formatted: Studies of emergent abilities catalogue capabilities that appear absent in smaller or less-trained models and then present, sharply, in larger or further-trained ones <ref type="bibr" target="#b39">(Srivastava et al., 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b44">Wei et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: The question has practical consequences, since an ability that arrives abruptly, including an unwanted one, arrives without warning.
A prominent critique answered that many of these jumps are illusions of measurement.
A test that scores each answer simply right or wrong can turn smooth improvement into an apparent leap (Schaeffer et al., 2023).
text.formatted: A test that scores each answer simply right or wrong can turn smooth improvement into an apparent leap <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">(Schaeffer et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: Case studies of models' internal structure show that some transitions are real.
Small models abruptly acquire an internal circuit for reusing patterns from earlier in a passage (Olsson et al., 2022).
text.formatted: Small models abruptly acquire an internal circuit for reusing patterns from earlier in a passage <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">(Olsson et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: Networks trained on arithmetic suddenly shift from memorizing to generalizing (Nanda et al., 2023; Power et al., 2022), and language models acquire syntax-sensitive internal structure in a brief window (Chen et al., 2024).
text.formatted: Networks trained on arithmetic suddenly shift from memorizing to generalizing <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">(Nanda et al., 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">Power et al., 2022)</ref>, and language models acquire syntax-sensitive internal structure in a brief window <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">(Chen et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Each of these studies, however, built its own instruments for its own case, and the findings do not combine into a general method.
A notable feature of this exchange is that both sides argue about whether trajectories contain discontinuities without a shared method for detecting discontinuities in trajectories.
No existing approach specifies how many phases a capability's growth contains, where the boundaries fall, or whether different capabilities follow different schedules.
At present, whether a curve is smooth or phased is judged plot by plot, by visual inspection.
The argument has a precedent.
For most of a century, developmental science asked whether infant development unfolds in discrete stages or continuously.
Stage theories treated each new skill as a sudden acquisition (Gesell, 1928; McGraw, 1943; Piaget, 1952).
text.formatted: Stage theories treated each new skill as a sudden acquisition <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">(Gesell, 1928;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">McGraw, 1943;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">Piaget, 1952)</ref>.

text.text: Dynamic systems theories treated new behaviors as gradual accumulations of strength, control, and attention, with apparent jumps arising when change in one component tips the whole system.

The newborn stepping reflex disappears as leg mass changes, and reaching advances and retreats as motor and perceptual systems come into alignment (Adolph & Robinson, 2008; Corbetta & Snapp-Childs, 2009; Thelen & Smith, 1994).
text.formatted: The newborn stepping reflex disappears as leg mass changes, and reaching advances and retreats as motor and perceptual systems come into alignment <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">(Adolph & Robinson, 2008;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">Corbetta & Snapp-Childs, 2009;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b40">Thelen & Smith, 1994)</ref>.

text.text: The field settled on an answer that dissolves the dichotomy.
Development is both, depending on the level of description.
Skills improve continuously, with no jumps between discrete states, yet the pace of improvement changes at particular ages (Adolph & Hoch, 2019; Spencer et al., 2011).
text.formatted: Skills improve continuously, with no jumps between discrete states, yet the pace of improvement changes at particular ages <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">(Adolph & Hoch, 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b38">Spencer et al., 2011)</ref>.

text.text: A phase, in this view, is a stretch of a continuous curve with its own rate of growth.
The productive question is no longer whether growth is smooth or stage-like, but when its pace changes and by how much, and that question can be answered empirically.
Seen this way, infant motor development has three signatures.

Growth reorganizes at a few identifiable ages, around independent sitting, walking onset, and locomotor consolidation (Adolph, 1997; Adolph et al., 2012; WHO Multicentre Growth Reference Study Group, 2006).
text.formatted: Growth reorganizes at a few identifiable ages, around independent sitting, walking onset, and locomotor consolidation <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">(Adolph, 1997;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">Adolph et al., 2012;</ref> <ref type="bibr">WHO Multicentre Growth Reference Study Group, 2006)</ref>.

text.text: Domains follow their own timetables, since each reorganization opens a new learning space (Iverson, 2021; Libertus & Hauf, 2017).
text.formatted: Domains follow their own timetables, since each reorganization opens a new learning space <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">(Iverson, 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">Libertus & Hauf, 2017)</ref>.

text.text: Sitting frees the hands for object exploration (Soska et al., 2010), and walking changes what infants see and how caregivers talk to them, with consequences for language (Kretch et al., 2014; Schneider & Iverson, 2022; Walle & Campos, 2014).
text.formatted: Sitting frees the hands for object exploration <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">(Soska et al., 2010)</ref>, and walking changes what infants see and how caregivers talk to them, with consequences for language <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">(Kretch et al., 2014;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b35">Schneider & Iverson, 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b42">Walle & Campos, 2014)</ref>.

text.text: Finally, individual infants differ in pace along a continuous landscape rather than sorting into types (Adolph & Hoch, 2019; Smith & Thelen, 2003).
text.formatted: Finally, individual infants differ in pace along a continuous landscape rather than sorting into types <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">(Adolph & Hoch, 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">Smith & Thelen, 2003)</ref>.

text.text: Developmental science also built the statistics to detect these signatures: growth-curve models, changepoint models, and spline-based models of growth (Cudeck & Klebe, 2002; Grimm et al., 2011; Harring et al., 2021; Howe et al., 2016).
text.formatted: Developmental science also built the statistics to detect these signatures: growth-curve models, changepoint models, and spline-based models of growth <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">(Cudeck & Klebe, 2002;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">Grimm et al., 2011;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">Harring et al., 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">Howe et al., 2016)</ref>.

text.text: These were recently combined into a single pipeline that, applied to a longitudinal infant sample, recovered transition ages from the data that matched known motor milestones and showed that individual differences in growth rate are substantial (An et al., 2026).
text.formatted: These were recently combined into a single pipeline that, applied to a longitudinal infant sample, recovered transition ages from the data that matched known motor milestones and showed that individual differences in growth rate are substantial <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">(An et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: Machine learning and developmental science already trade ideas in both directions.

Developmental robotics has long drawn on infancy research (Cangelosi & Schlesinger, 2018; Oudeyer & Smith, 2016), and language models are now trained on child-sized or childperspective data (Frank, 2023; Hu et al., 2024; Vong et al., 2024; Warstadt et al., 2025).
text.formatted: Developmental robotics has long drawn on infancy research <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">(Cangelosi & Schlesinger, 2018;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">Oudeyer & Smith, 2016)</ref>, and language models are now trained on child-sized or childperspective data <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">(Frank, 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">Hu et al., 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b41">Vong et al., 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b43">Warstadt et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: The exchange has not yet included developmental science's trajectory statistics, the methods built for precisely the curve-shape question on which the emergence debate turns.

The aim of the present study is to establish whether the capability growth of language models has the phase structure that developmental science found in infants, and to do so with the same statistical test.

To that end, we take the infant pipeline of An et al. (2026) and apply it to language model training trajectories, treating models as participants, checkpoints as visits, and benchmarks as developmental domains.
text.formatted: To that end, we take the infant pipeline of <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">An et al. (2026)</ref> and apply it to language model training trajectories, treating models as participants, checkpoints as visits, and benchmarks as developmental domains.

text.text: In essence, the current study is a transfer of a validated developmental method to a new population of learners.
It follows the tradition of computational work that brings developmental data and methods to bear on language models (Frank, 2023; Vong et al., 2024).
text.formatted: It follows the tradition of computational work that brings developmental data and methods to bear on language models <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">(Frank, 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b41">Vong et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Three questions guide the work.
First, does a phase-structured model describe the growth of capabilities over training better than smooth alternatives?
Second, where do the transitions fall, and do they differ across domains?
Third, how much do individual models differ in developmental rate, independent of their initial level?
The data come from the Pythia suite (Biderman et al., 2023), a family of 16 language models released so that researchers can study how models change over training.
text.formatted: The data come from the Pythia suite <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">(Biderman et al., 2023)</ref>, a family of 16 language models released so that researchers can study how models change over training.

text.text: The suite spans eight sizes, from 70 million to 12 billion parameters, each trained in two versions: one on a large public text collection and one on a copy with duplicate documents removed.
Every model saw the same text in the same order, so the models differ principally in size, a stable and exactly measured constitutional variable of a kind unavailable in human samples.
Model weights were saved at 154 checkpoints.

The suite's released evaluations, computed with a standard opensource evaluation toolkit (Gao et al., 2023), cover 27 of them, densely spaced early in training and every 10,000 steps later on, with no evaluated checkpoint between steps 3,000 and 13,000.
text.formatted: The suite's released evaluations, computed with a standard opensource evaluation toolkit <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">(Gao et al., 2023)</ref>, cover 27 of them, densely spaced early in training and every 10,000 steps later on, with no evaluated checkpoint between steps 3,000 and 13,000.

text.text: One observation is one benchmark score for one model at one checkpoint, and each per-task analysis draws on 16 models × 27 checkpoints = 432 observations, close in size to the perdomain analyses of the infant study (433 observations).
In developmental terms, each model is a participant, each checkpoint is a visit, and each benchmark is a standardized assessment administered identically at every visit (Table 1).
text.formatted: In developmental terms, each model is a participant, each checkpoint is a visit, and each benchmark is a standardized assessment administered identically at every visit (Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_0">1</ref>).

text.text: We take the logarithm of the training step as the developmental clock, since early training, like early infancy, contains a disproportionate share of change.
Training steps index accumulated experience rather than maturation, since nothing changes in these systems except through learning.
The mapping is therefore an analogy about the shape of learning trajectories, not a claim that the mechanisms are the same.
Five benchmarks serve as developmental domains.

text.text: Like the motor domains of the infant study, these tasks tap distinguishable capacities that could develop on different schedules.
A documented audit selected these five from the released evaluations, excluding tasks that never rise above chance or lack early coverage.
One excluded near-chance task, ARC-Challenge, was retained as a comparison case in the robustness analysis.

The phase-structured model outperformed all four conventional alternatives on every task (Table 2).

text.text: The margins over the linear and logarithmic curves were decisive by any convention, and the logarithmic curve, which represents the hypothesis that capability simply accelerates early and then levels off, fit worst of all.
The cubic polynomial was the closest competitor, as expected, since the spline is itself built from cubic segments.

Nonetheless, on four of the five tasks the spline's margin over the cubic was roughly 10 times the corresponding margin in the infant study, and that margin survives a conservative correction for the knot search.
Winogrande is the exception.
Its small margin over the cubic does not survive the correction, so we classify four tasks, rather than five, as decisively phase-structured and defer Winogrande's status to the robustness analysis.
The data-selected transitions occupied a shared set of training steps, deployed domainspecifically (Table 3).
text.formatted: The data-selected transitions occupied a shared set of training steps, deployed domainspecifically (Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_2">3</ref>).

text.text: Three tasks placed their transitions near steps 3,000 and 13,000.
SciQ, the knowledge task, reorganized earliest, near steps 1,000 and 13,000, and Winogrande selected only a single, weakly determined late knot.
The independent fits sharpened this picture (Table 4).
text.formatted: The independent fits sharpened this picture (Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_3">4</ref>).

text.text: Nearly every individual curve preferred the phase-structured model, and the few exceptions were trajectories that remained near chance, precisely where no phase structure should exist.

On SciQ, most models selected the identical configuration, and the four structured tasks concentrated their first transitions within the first few thousand steps and their second within the tens of thousands.
Winogrande's independent knots were distributed across the whole training run with no agreement, which converts the pooled analysis's uncertainty into a clear conclusion.
This task has no robust transition within the training window, and it serves as an internal negative control.
One size-related pattern also emerged.
On two tasks, the models that exited their rapid-growth phase latest were the smallest.
Within-phase rates followed a consistent shape (Table 3).
text.formatted: Within-phase rates followed a consistent shape (Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_2">3</ref>).

text.text: On the four structured tasks, growth began slowly, accelerated to several times the initial rate in a middle phase, and then decelerated, with confidence intervals that did not overlap across phases.
This is the slow-fastslow signature the infant study described as grounding, expanding, and mastering (An et al., 2026).
text.formatted: This is the slow-fastslow signature the infant study described as grounding, expanding, and mastering <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">(An et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: The tasks ended training in different phases.
SciQ decelerated almost to zero, the profile of a consolidating capability.
Winogrande was still accelerating when training ended, the profile of a capability whose expansion phase was interrupted by the end of the training budget.
Note.

text.text: Individual differences in developmental rate exist and are reliable.
On every task, a model that allowed each learner its own growth rate fit the data decisively better than a model that gave all learners the same rate (Table 5).
text.formatted: On every task, a model that allowed each learner its own growth rate fit the data decisively better than a model that gave all learners the same rate (Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_4">5</ref>).

text.text: The share of score variance attributable to stable differences between models varied by domain.
It was smallest on SciQ, the knowledge task, where all 16 learners followed nearly the same track, and largest on the reasoning-weighted tasks, where the learners spread apart.
Language models, like infants, do not all travel the same curve at the same speed (An et al., 2026).
text.formatted: Language models, like infants, do not all travel the same curve at the same speed <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">(An et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: Pace was independent of starting point.
Before the first transition, the 16 models were nearly indistinguishable in accuracy, and the small variation in starting level that did exist did not predict a model's later rate on any task.
The faster learners were not the ones with an early advantage.
The infant study reached a parallel conclusion by a different route.
Infants varied in their starting levels, and those starting levels did not predict how fast they grew (An et al., 2026).
text.formatted: Infants varied in their starting levels, and those starting levels did not predict how fast they grew <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">(An et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: In both populations, how fast a learner develops cannot be read from where it begins.
The source of the rate differences is where the two populations diverge.
The infant study established that rate differences exist but could not identify their source, given the complexity of human development.
In the language models, by contrast, parameter count and environment were strictly controlled.
Each model's growth rate correlated almost perfectly with the logarithm of its parameter count on every task (Table 5).
text.formatted: Each model's growth rate correlated almost perfectly with the logarithm of its parameter count on every task (Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_4">5</ref>).

text.text: Larger models developed faster, and size alone accounted for nearly all of the variation in pace.
The training variants make the same point from the other direction.

Two models of the same size trained on different data, an environmental manipulation, developed at nearly identical rates, so the environmental difference affected pace far less than constitution did.
A small residual remains.
The share of rate variance that size does not explain is an estimate of individuality that the scaling-law framework does not represent (Kaplan et al., 2020).
text.formatted: The share of rate variance that size does not explain is an estimate of individuality that the scaling-law framework does not represent <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">(Kaplan et al., 2020)</ref>.

text.text: Infants and models therefore agree that learners differ in pace and that the difference is not a matter of starting point.
They differ in how much of that pace can be attributed to a single measured cause, and this difference reflects the two study designs more than the learners themselves.
The measurement critique holds that apparent jumps come from scoring answers right or wrong (Schaeffer et al., 2023).
text.formatted: The measurement critique holds that apparent jumps come from scoring answers right or wrong <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">(Schaeffer et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: Two checks address it.
Refit on the logit of accuracy, the four interpretable tasks selected exactly the same transitions, with the same near-chance exceptions.
Refit on LAMBADA perplexity, the continuous measure, the phase structure did not weaken.
It became more pronounced, with larger margins over every smooth alternative and nearunanimous agreement among the independent fits (Supplementary Tables S1 to S4).
text.formatted: It became more pronounced, with larger margins over every smooth alternative and nearunanimous agreement among the independent fits (Supplementary Tables <ref type="table" target="#tab_3">S1 to S4</ref>).

text.text: The one difference concerned timing.
The perplexity transitions fell about a decade of log-steps earlier than the accuracy transitions (Figure 1).
text.formatted: The perplexity transitions fell about a decade of log-steps earlier than the accuracy transitions (Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_1">1</ref>).

text.text: The reason is visible in the raw curves.

Accuracy remains at zero until the model's best guess is correct often enough to register, so the threshold metric delays the appearance of a transition that is already underway in the underlying predictions.
Threshold scoring therefore does not create the transition.
It delays its detection.
Note.
Thin lines show the 16 models on accuracy (top) and perplexity (bottom), the solid line shows the population curve, and dashed vertical lines mark the data-selected transitions.
The perplexity transitions precede the accuracy transitions by roughly one decade of log-steps.
An analysis pipeline built for infants, applied to language models with only the time axis changed, paralleled the infant findings.
Growth in these systems appears to be continuous, with no jumps between discrete states, yet its pace changes at a few identifiable points.
It proceeds slowly while foundations form, rapidly during a period of expansion, and slowly again as a capability consolidates.
Different capabilities keep different schedules, with knowledge reorganizing before reasoning.
Furthermore, individual learners follow the same course at reliably different speeds.
This is the resolution developmental science reached for infants.
The productive question is not whether growth is smooth or stepwise, but when its pace changes and by how much, and the same resolution is available to the emergence debate.
This resolution speaks to both sides of that debate.
The jumps are not illusions, since phase structure survives and becomes more pronounced on a continuous measure.
Nor are the jumps discontinuities, since abilities do not appear instantaneously.
What appears as sudden emergence on a capability test is the delayed expression of a gradual transition that began, on the underlying measure, well before the test could register it.
An evaluation that relies on threshold scores alone will detect a capability's expansion phase only after it is already underway.
One finding had no infant counterpart.
Rate differences in infants are substantial and unexplained.
Rate differences in language models, by contrast, reduce almost entirely to a single measured cause, parameter count, with training data contributing far less.
Human development takes place in a complex ecological system in which both biological and environmental factors play a role.
Computational models, by contrast, develop with constitution measured exactly and environments held constant.
The two types of learners therefore complement each other in design, and each answers a question the other cannot.
Learners with no body, no brain, no biological maturation, and no social partners nonetheless grow in phases.
Shared trajectory shape, however, does not imply shared mechanism.
Infants generate their own curriculum through action, and these models receive a fixed one.
What the results show is that the growth of both is phase-structured, domain-timed, and individually variable in ways that one statistical framework captures.
The paper makes three contributions.

First, it gives the emergence debate a formal test with three criteria: whether a phase-structured model outperforms smooth alternatives, whether independent learners agree on where the phases fall, and whether the transitions survive changes of metric.
The present data met all three criteria.
Second, it provides a construct mapping from infant development to model training, so that participants, visits, domains, and constitution have counterparts on both sides.
In turn, the same pipeline can be applied to both learners.

Third, it reports a direct comparison of infant and language-model growth conducted with identical methods, including one result the infant design could not produce, the decomposition of developmental rate against an exactly measured constitutional variable.
Two implications follow for how models are evaluated.
A training run may be better assessed as a trajectory than as an endpoint.
A capability's phase at the end of training is itself diagnostic.
A capability still accelerating when training stops, as one was in the present data, is a capability whose expansion the training budget cut short, and endpoint testing cannot detect this.
A capability also changes its growth rate as it enters the expansion phase, before the capability is fully present.
Trajectory monitoring could therefore give advance warning that an ability, including an unwanted one, is approaching.
For developmental science, the benefit flows in the opposite direction.

Model suites offer dense, complete longitudinal data in a population where development can be rerun with the environment changed, so timing, cascade, and sensitiveperiod hypotheses that infant data can support only correlationally become directly testable.

Transitions here also partially align with a global change in training conditions, much as infant transitions align with re-gating events such as walking onset (Adolph & Tamis-LeMonda, 2014; Iverson, 2021).
text.formatted: Transitions here also partially align with a global change in training conditions, much as infant transitions align with re-gating events such as walking onset <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">(Adolph & Tamis-LeMonda, 2014;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">Iverson, 2021)</ref>.

text.text: This alignment suggests a question the two fields can investigate together: how system-wide changes in the conditions of learning organize domain-specific reorganization.
Each limitation of the present study points to a direction for future work.
First, the sample is one model family with 16 members organized as eight near-duplicate pairs, so the recovered transition steps are properties of this training regime until replicated.
The public release of the analysis pipeline makes replication immediately feasible for other openly released model suites.
Second, all five domains belong to a single modality, language, which is narrower than the infant battery's coverage of motor and perceptual domains.
Expansion to other learning domains and types of learners is therefore the natural next step.
Third, the released evaluations omitted the stretch of training between steps 3,000 and 13,000, which limits how precisely the second transition can be located.
Evaluating the saved checkpoints within that gap would locate it more precisely.
Finally, this study is observational.
It describes the shape of development without intervening on it.
Future studies could introduce small, well-timed training experiences and measure whether they redirect the trajectory, as an analogue of brief parent-guided motor practice (An & Libertus, 2025).
text.formatted: Future studies could introduce small, well-timed training experiences and measure whether they redirect the trajectory, as an analogue of brief parent-guided motor practice <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">(An & Libertus, 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Whether the path from an untrained model to a trained one is smooth or phase-structured no longer needs to be judged by visual inspection.
Applied to a population of 16 artificial learners, methods built for infants give a formal answer.
Growth is phase-structured, by decisive margins, on every measure examined.
Two very different kinds of learners grow in the same shape, and developmental science already possesses the tools to measure it.
change at specific points, called knots.
Between knots the curve is smooth.
At a knot, the growth rate is allowed to shift.
The positions of the knots were not chosen by the researcher.
A grid search evaluated every eligible checkpoint location and selected the configuration using standard information criteria, which score a model's fit while penalizing its complexity.
The resulting phase-structured model was then compared against four conventional curves that allow no rate changes (linear, quadratic, cubic, and logarithmic).
The same procedure yielded the average growth rate within each phase, and mixed-effects models tested whether individual models differed reliably in their growth rates.

The analysis is a direct port of the infant pipeline ofAn et al. (2026), with the time axis, knot grid, and spacing constraints adapted to the training clock and everything else unchanged.Three robustness checks accompany the main results.

Second, the pipeline was refit on the logit of accuracy, a transformation that removes the boundedness of percent-correct scores.
Third, for LAMBADA, the one task whose released evaluations include a continuous measure, the pipeline was refit on perplexity.
Perplexity indexes how poorly a model predicts the correct text, so lower values indicate better performance.
Accuracy is what remains of this continuous quantity after each answer is scored as right or wrong.
